title: The year
hookLine: zakat is due when wealth has been held a full lunar year

lines: A THIN SILVER LINE AT DUSK.
cards: On the evening the new moon is first seen, someone steps outside, looks low on the horizon, and finds it: a thin silver line, barely there. A month has begun.

Muslims have watched for that line for the start of Ramadan and the days of Hajj. It's also the clock for something less well-known. Money in a savings account doesn't announce when zakat is due on it.
No bill comes in the mail. The only reminder is the moon going around, month after month, until a whole year of moons has passed over what you hold. The word for that year: hawl.

teach.h: NOT DUE UNTIL A YEAR PASSES.
teach.b: First, the rule. A hadith in the Sunan of Abu Dawud, with a similar one in at-Tirmidhi, says that no zakat is due on wealth until the hawl, the year, has passed over it.
Wealth has to stay with you a full year before it's counted. Money that arrives and leaves in a season isn't. Second, which year.
The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's words, "the number of the months with Allah is twelve months", and elsewhere calls the new moons fixed times for people.
The Islamic calendar follows those moons, so zakat's year is a year of moons.
And because the moon's year and the sun's don't line up, a zakat date fixed by the moon slides earlier on a wall calendar from one year to the next. Third, the exception.
A harvest doesn't wait for a year. The Qur'an tells farmers to give the due of their crops on the day of the harvest, and a later day on this path is about that. Fourth, the date itself.
Some Muslims set it to the day their wealth first crossed the threshold, and count a year of moons from there.

teach.h: THE NUMBER OF THE MONTHS WITH ALLAH IS TWELVE MONTHS.
teach.b: Some choose a day in Ramadan, so their giving falls in that month. And the schools of law differ on what happens if savings dip below the line partway through the year, so people ask a scholar they trust.
What these answers share is a date: one day a year when the whole of what you hold gets looked at, honestly, and a share goes out.

how: Muslims who pay zakat keep a yearly zakat date by the Islamic lunar calendar, some fixing it in Ramadan, and on that day total their zakatable wealth above the nisab.

games.q: you're a farmer. your grain comes in this week. you think: I'll wait a year and pay zakat on it with my savings. what does the Qur'an say?
o: wait the full year, like savings.
give its due on the day of the harvest.
games.why: give the due on the harvest day. the harvest doesn't wait for the hawl.

practice: Let a few candidates for a yearly date come up, a day in Ramadan, the start of a new year, a birthday, the day your savings first grew, and breathe with each one in turn.
When one feels like a day you'd actually keep, as your zakat date or, if zakat isn't yours, a day for looking honestly at what you have, let it stay.

wordCard.voice: Hawl. The year that wealth must be held before zakat is due, counted in moons. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the year that must pass over wealth before zakat is due.

carryVoice: Your line: a yearly date. Next comes what gets counted: gold, trade, crops and herds. See you tomorrow.
